slot.brief: Two straightforward universal statements (e.g., all A are B, all B are C) followed by two conclusions; ask which conclusions logically follow, with clearly valid/invalid options.

stem:
**Statements:**
All pens are books.
All books are tables.

**Conclusions:**
I. All pens are tables.
II. All tables are books.

verdicts.working: Let P = pens, B = books, T = tables. Statements: P ⊆ B and B ⊆ T. By transitivity, P ⊆ T, so Conclusion I ('All pens are tables') holds. B ⊆ T does not necessarily imply T ⊆ B, so Conclusion II does not follow. Therefore, only Conclusion I follows.

working:
All pens are books, and all books are tables. Chaining the two statements gives: all pens are tables. So I follows. For II, the statement 'All books are tables' cannot be reversed: tables may include items that are not books. Pens ⊂ books ⊂ tables is a valid diagram in which tables is the larger circle, so II does not follow. Only I follows.

Independent check: Let P = pens, B = books, T = tables. Statements: P ⊆ B and B ⊆ T. By transitivity, P ⊆ T, so Conclusion I ('All pens are tables') holds. B ⊆ T does not necessarily imply T ⊆ B, so Conclusion II does not follow. Therefore, only Conclusion I follows.
solution:
Let P = pens, B = books, T = tables. The statements give $P \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq T$.
$$P \subseteq B \subseteq T \Rightarrow P \subseteq T$$
So I follows (All-All-All syllogism).
II is the converse of 'All books are tables', and a universal affirmative cannot be reversed. Tables can be a larger set than books, so II does not follow. Only I follows, which is (A).
